docs.title: Run the example factory to a merged PR

beats.act: Open the project forge already manages
beats.say: This is the ground the whole story stands on: a real CLI with a real test suite, already onboarded, already merged through once. Nothing here is seeded — the roadmap, the history and the contract are what the previous cycles left behind.

beats.act: Press "Architect →"
beats.say: The operator has a feature in mind and no plan for it. That is what the Architect is for, and it is the only entry point in the product that starts from a sentence rather than from an initiative that already exists.

beats.act: Describe the work, cap what this run may spend, and press "Start architect"
beats.say: The ceiling is set before the work starts, not discovered afterwards. Pressing Start mints a session and names it on the page the operator is standing on, so the run is nameable before anything navigates.

do.with: Add an --exclude-author <pattern> flag: the inverse of --author. Same *-wildcard, case-insensitive matching, repeatable and OR-combined. It composes with every other filter. State the precedence explicitly when --author and --exclude-author are both given, and annotate the text header and the JSON output the way --author already does.

beats.act: Open the session and answer the Architect's questions
beats.say: The interview is where the operator's one sentence becomes something buildable. The answers are not decoration — the precedence rule stated here is the clause the review will come back to.

repeat.with: The gate command is `npm test`. Exclude wins over include when both are given — say so in the header annotation. Breaking the existing human-readable output is not acceptable; the new flag is additive, like --author was.

beats.act: Read the plan at the gate and approve it
beats.say: This is the first of the two human gates. The operator reads what will be built and what it will touch, and approving arms the work — the plan is committed and the gate is no longer waiting on anyone.

beats.act: Go back to the project the plan belongs to
beats.say: The plan is approved. The operator goes back to the project to start the work it planned.

beats.act: Start the scheduler so queued work can be claimed
beats.say: Planning and building are done by a scheduler that claims queued work. Nothing the operator enqueues moves until it is running, and the product says so plainly rather than leaving the work to sit — so starting it is part of the journey, not setup hidden behind it.

beats.act: Watch the factory plan and build the initiative
beats.say: Starting the scheduler was the operator's last act for a while. The factory claims the initiative, decomposes it into work items, builds them and stops at the review gate — unattended, and faster than the operator could have driven it. What the operator does next is not start the work; it is READ it.

beats.act: Open the initiative to find the run it produced
beats.say: The card says the work is ready for review. The operator opens it to reach the run itself — and the drawer names the cycle that produced it, which is the handle everything downstream is keyed by. The initiative is what was asked for; the cycle is what actually ran.

beats.act: Hand the plan to the build flow
beats.say: The architect has planned and stopped, which is where it is meant to stop — the plan is the first thing a human is asked to approve. Starting development is a separate act, and this is the operator making it: the same initiative, repointed from the flow that decomposed it to the flow that builds it.

wait.boundBasis: MAX_DECLARED_WAIT_MS binding at 1800000 ms; ground.budget_usd $44 at the measured $0.5029/min would afford 5249123 ms

beats.act: Watch the run build
beats.say: The dev station fans out over the work items the plan decomposed into. Each row on the timeline is a station with its own status and its own cost, so "what is it doing and what has it spent" is one screen, not an investigation.

beats.act: The built work is assembled for review
beats.say: Between building and judging there is a step that puts the change together with the evidence for it — the diff, the acceptance criteria and what was actually demonstrated. The reviewer reads that, not a pile of commits.

beats.act: The review station finishes its pass
beats.say: A machine reviewer goes first, against the acceptance criteria and the change class the plan gate confirmed. Its pass runs inside the same cycle the operator has already been watching, and finishes without asking anything of them.

beats.act: The review findings are on the run page
beats.say: Its findings are the reviewer's starting point, not its verdict — the human decides.

beats.act: Open the review verdict at its gate
beats.say: The review has an opinion and the operator goes to read it where the decision is made.

beats.act: Anchor one blocking comment to the precedence criterion (the first criterion, said so in the log, when none names precedence) and send it back
beats.say: This is the send-back the whole story is built around. The operator does not restart anything and does not write a work item — they anchor one blocking comment to the criterion it fails, and that comment becomes the acceptance criterion the fix has to meet.

do.with: The precedence when both --author and --exclude-author are given is not stated in the output. Exclude must win, and the header annotation must say how many commits each filter removed, so a zero-commit report is never ambiguous about which filter emptied it.

beats.act: The fix lands on the same branch and comes back for re-review
beats.say: No restart, no second cycle, no lost work. The send-back became one more thing to satisfy on the branch that already exists, which is the difference between a review loop and a do-over.

beats.act: Open the re-reviewed verdict at its gate
beats.say: The fix came back. The operator reads the verdict again before deciding.

beats.act: Read the fix against the criterion, and resolve the blocking comment it answers (the first criterion's, said so in the log, when none names precedence)
beats.say: The operator does not take the reviewer's word that the fix landed — they read it against the exact criterion the send-back named, on the same comment they anchored there, and resolve it. With no blocking comments left, the gate itself has nothing left to derive but approve.

beats.act: Approve — which is the merge
beats.say: The second human gate, and the only one that spends something irreversible. Approving is not a signal to a later step — it IS the merge, so the operator is pressing the button that lands the change.

wait.boundBasis: MAX_DECLARED_WAIT_MS binding at 1800000 ms; ground.budget_usd $44 at the measured $0.5029/min would afford 5249123 ms

beats.act: Reflect on the cycle
beats.say: The cycle ends by writing down what it learned. The operator answers every question the reflector asked — a pick where it offered options, a note where it did not — and that hands the reflector one more pass to fold the answers into the brain.

beats.act: Open the knowledge graph
beats.say: The cycle is done. Before reading what it learned, the operator opens the knowledge graph.

beats.act: Find what the cycle learned on the knowledge graph
beats.say: The theme the reflector wrote is now a node the next planner will read. That is the loop closing: this cycle made the project's brain bigger, and nobody typed it in.

beats.act: Open the flows index
beats.say: Before checking what the run cost, the operator opens the flows this factory runs.

beats.act: Check what the run cost
beats.say: One figure, and it is the same figure the event log holds. A run that cannot say honestly what it spent cannot be trusted with a ceiling, so this is checked against the log rather than taken from the screen.

beats.act: ACT 2 — open the projects index to start a second initiative
beats.say: A second, smaller change starts the same way the first one did: from the projects the operator already manages.

beats.act: ACT 2 — open gitpulse again
beats.say: The same ground, a second time — nothing here was reset between the two initiatives.

beats.act: ACT 2 — press "Architect →" for the second idea
beats.say: The first change already merged. The operator has a second, smaller one in mind.

beats.act: ACT 2 — describe the second idea and start its architect
beats.say: A smaller ceiling for a smaller idea, set before the work starts.

do.with: Add --sort <column>[:asc|:desc] to the coupling report, matching the flag the tags and authors/compare reports already accept (src/sort.ts). Register coupling's own sortable columns (file, otherFile, count) the same way the other reports do, default to count:desc when no direction is given, and apply it to both the plain-text and --json row order. Document the flag in the coupling section of README next to the other two.

beats.act: ACT 2 — open the session and answer the second interview
beats.say: A smaller idea, the same interview shape — the architect decides how many rounds it needs.

repeat.with: The gate command is `npm test`. Default the sort direction per column the way the other two reports already do (numeric desc, text asc) — do not invent a new default for coupling. Breaking the existing plain-text or --json output when --sort is absent is not acceptable; the flag is additive, like the first one was.

beats.act: ACT 2 — read the second plan at the gate and approve it
beats.say: Approving the plan is what mints the second initiative — the same act that started the first.

beats.act: ACT 2 — go back to the project for the second initiative
beats.say: Back to the project to start the second initiative, exactly as the first one was started.

beats.act: ACT 2 — return to the roadmap; the scheduler is still running from ACT 1
beats.say: The scheduler never stopped between the two initiatives — there is nothing to start again.

beats.act: ACT 2 — watch the factory plan and build the second initiative
beats.say: The second initiative is smaller, but it is planned and built the same unattended way the first one was.

beats.act: ACT 2 — open the second initiative to find the run it produced
beats.say: A second run, with its own cycle id — nothing about it is the first run under a different name.

beats.act: ACT 2 — hand the second plan to the build flow
beats.say: Development starts on the second initiative too — and this time the operator does not wait for it to finish.

beats.act: ACT 2 — open the flows index to watch the second run build
beats.say: Before catching the run mid-flight, the operator opens the flow that is building it.

beats.act: ACT 2 — open the develop flow monitor
beats.say: This is the surface with per-work-item evidence — the run's own detail page has none.

beats.act: ACT 2 — wait for the second run's first work item to start
beats.say: Something is genuinely in flight before anything is interrupted — otherwise stopping mid-flight proves nothing.

wait.boundBasis: MAX_DECLARED_WAIT_MS binding at 1800000 ms; ground.budget_usd $44 at the measured $0.5029/min would afford 5249123 ms

beats.act: ACT 2 — open the second run's own detail page
beats.say: Act 2 starts where Act 1 was watched from: the operator opens the run they are about to stop.

beats.act: ACT 2 — stop the second run mid-flight
beats.say: Things stop halfway. What matters is not that it never happens but that stopping is a decision the operator makes on purpose — and that it never throws away the work already done.

wait.boundBasis: MAX_DECLARED_WAIT_MS binding at 1800000 ms; ground.budget_usd $44 at the measured $0.5029/min would afford 5249123 ms

beats.act: ACT 2 — step away while the halt lands
beats.say: The runner needs a moment to reach the boundary it halts at.

beats.act: ACT 2 — after the halt, the running work item finished naturally
beats.say: The work item already in flight when the operator stopped the run is not thrown away mid-turn — it finishes, because nothing in this product aborts a live turn.

wait.boundBasis: MAX_DECLARED_WAIT_MS binding at 1800000 ms; ground.budget_usd $44 at the measured $0.5029/min would afford 5249123 ms

beats.act: ACT 2 — and the next work item never started at all
beats.say: That is the fact a resume has to prove it does not skip — not an assumption this story is making about it.

beats.act: ACT 2 — open the second run's own detail page again
beats.say: Back to the run itself to confirm why it stopped, and then to resume it.

beats.act: ACT 2 — confirm the stopped, resumable state
beats.say: The product says plainly why this run stopped — not a crash, an operator decision — and that it is still here to resume.

beats.act: ACT 2 — resume via the run's own resume control
beats.say: Resume is not a fresh start. It picks up from what the stop preserved — the worktree, the branch, the work items already done.

beats.act: ACT 2 — step back to the monitor to watch the resumed run
beats.say: The second attempt starts from what the first one finished, not from nothing.

beats.act: ACT 2 — the finished work item survived the stop and the resume
beats.say: The work item that passed is still passed and its commits are still on the branch — that is the whole reason a stopped run is recoverable rather than wasted.

wait.boundBasis: MAX_DECLARED_WAIT_MS binding at 1800000 ms; ground.budget_usd $44 at the measured $0.5029/min would afford 5249123 ms

beats.act: ACT 2 — the unfinished work item resumes, not skipped
beats.say: A stopped run does not skip the work it never reached — it comes back and finishes it. The story ends here: it does not wait for this second, resumed run to merge.
